text:
B: Hello, can you hear me? I am Bożena.
A: Yeah. Alright. Callum.
B: Hello, Callum. Where do you live, if I can ask?
A: Swindon.
B: Swindon. I am in Southampton. This is my last call, I think. And for you?
A: Yeah, last one.
B: Good, then we are both, erm, experts now. What do you do, Callum?
A: Nothing at the minute. Took redundancy from a sports shop. Assistant manager. Looking for warehouse jobs.
B: Ah, warehouse. My son works in logistics, near Reading. A big distribution centre, for a supermarket. He started on the shifts and now he is, how you say, a team leader. He says the first month is hard, and after that is okay.
A: Yeah? What did he do before?
B: Before? Erm, he did a little bit of everything. A phone shop, a restaurant. He did not know what he wanted. I worried very much. And then, suddenly, he is happy. So it happens.
A: Right. That's good.
B: You have been looking long?
A: Four months. Bit half-hearted, to be honest. Everyone today's told me to change my CV, so I'm gonna do that tonight. Probably.
B: Probably! You sound like my son. He says probably, and I know it means next week.
A: Ha. Yeah. Fair.
B: I am also not working. I was pharmacy technician, and the branch closed in 2023. Two years, nearly. So I cannot tell you off, I think.
A: Do you miss it?
B: Do I miss it? Erm, the people, yes, very much. The regulars. Not so much the computer systems, head office changed them every year. You miss your shop?
A: Yeah, more than I thought. The lads I worked with, mainly. Having somewhere to be. Like, you just turn up and you know what you're doing. Now it's just sort of, I'm in the house all day, PlayStation, Greggs on the way back from the job centre. Days just go.
B: Yes. I understand this. The days go and you think, what did I do today? For me the church helps, the coffee morning, my walks by the river. Something with a time. You have someone at home?
A: Girlfriend. Jess. She's a dental nurse.
B: A dental nurse, very good, steady job. She is patient with you?
A: Yeah. Mostly. She's been good about it.
B: Then you are lucky. And I am sure she wants you happy, not only working. Is this okay, am I asking too much?
A: Nah, it's fine.
B: My husband, Tomasz, when the pharmacy closed, he said, Bożena, you worked since you were nineteen, rest a little. But I did not like to rest. I made pierogi, so many, the freezer is full until next Christmas.
A: Ha. That's a lot of pierogi.
B: Too many. My grandchildren like them, so is okay. You like Polish food?
A: Never really had it. I'm a bit plain. Chicken, pasta, that.
B: Pierogi is just pasta with potato inside. You would like it, I think, with—
